ABSTRACT
Background: The interrelationships between physical activity (PA), sleep disorders, and
hypertension remain incompletely characterised, particularly regarding potential
interactions between PA and sleep disorders on hypertension risk. This study aimed to
investigate these associations using complementary epidemiological approaches.
Methods: We conducted a population-based observational analysis of 18,052 adults
aged ≥18 years using data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey,
a nationally representative cross-sectional survey (2005–2018). Weighted multivariate
logistic regression models were used to examine the associations between PA, sleep
disorders, and hypertension, as well as the interaction effect of PA and sleep disorders
on hypertension. Additionally, we performed a two-sample Mendelian randomisation
(MR) analysis was conducted to assess the causal relationship between PA, sleep
disorders, and hypertension.
Results: The analysis of observational data shows that sleep disorders are significantly
associated with a higher risk of hypertension, with an odds ratio (OR) of 1.61 (95% CI:
1.10–2.35, p = 0.015). Restricted Cubic Spline (RCS) analysis revealed an S-shaped
dose-response relationship between PA and hypertension (P-non-linear < 0.001). The
MR analysis results were consistent with these findings.
Conclusions: Convergent evidence from observational and genetic analyses identified
sleep disorders as an independent risk factor for hypertension. The non-monotonic
S-shaped association between PA and hypertension underscored the importance of
personalised activity prescriptions for cardiovascular risk optimisation. Notably, no
significant interaction was observed between PA and sleep disorders, suggesting that
their effects on hypertension are likely independent.
PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY
This study integrated observational and genetic data (Mendelian randomisation) from
18,052 adults to investigate the relationships between physical activity (PA), sleep
disorders, and hypertension. Key findings demonstrate:
1. Non-Linear PA-Hypertension Association: Analyses revealed a significant S-shaped
dose-response relationship (P-non-linear <0.001) Both insufficient and excessive PA
were linked to higher hypertension risk, challenging linear assumptions.
2. Causal Role of PA Intensity: Genetic analyses confirmed causal protective effects
of light and vigorous-intensity PA on hypertension risk. Findings also indicated a
need for re-evaluation of moderate-intensity PA recommendations.
3. Sleep Disorders as an Independent Risk Factor : Sleep disorders significantly
increased hypertension risk (OR = 1.61, 95% CI:1.10–2.35, P = 0.015) .No significant
interaction with PA was found, indicating independent biological pathways.
In conclusion, sleep disorders are a key target for hypertension prevention alongside
PA. The non-monotonic relationship underscores the need for personalised PA
prescriptions. The lack of interaction suggests that sleep and PA interventions should
be implemented as distinct, parallel public health strategies. Future guidelines should
incorporate these findings..

Introduction
Hypertension, defined as systolic blood pressure ≥130 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure ≥80 mm
Hg [1], affects over 1.2 billion adults worldwide and remains a leading modifiable risk factor for
cardiovascular disease (CVD) and premature mortality [2]. Despite substantial advancements in
pharmacological therapies, the global burden of hypertension-related morbidity persists [3], under-
scoring the need to identify effective lifestyle-based interventions to complement existing therapies.
Among these, PA and sleep health have emerged as critical behavioural determinants of blood
pressure regulation [4]. However, the complex interplay between PA, sleep disorders, and hyper-
tension remains insufficiently characterised, particularly regarding dose-response relationships,
underlying causal mechanisms, and potential interactions—key gaps that limit the development of
precision prevention strategies.
Observational studies consistently associate higher PA levels with a lower risk of hypertension
[5], with proposed mechanisms including enhanced endothelial function, improved autonomic
nervous system regulation, reduced systemic inflammation, increased urinary sodium excretion,
and enhanced insulin sensitivity [6,7]. The World Health Organisation (WHO) recommends at least
150 min of moderate-intensity PA weekly for cardiovascular health [8], yet emerging evidence sug-
gests a nonlinear relationship between PA and hypertension [5]. However, emerging evidence
suggests a nonlinear relationship between PA and hypertension, where excessive PA may paradox-
ically increase blood pressure due to oxidative stress and arterial stiffness, challenging the traditional
‘more is better’ paradigm [9]. Simultaneously, Sleep disorders have been implicated in hypertension
pathogenesis through mechanisms such as sympathetic nervous system hyperactivity,
hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis dysregulation, and circadian rhythm disturbances [10].
Regular PA has been shown to improve sleep quality and cardiovascular autonomic control, thereby
contributing to blood pressure regulation [11,12]. Despite these well-established individual associ-
ations, limited research has examined whether PA and Sleep disorders interact synergistically or
antagonistically in influencing hypertension risk. This oversight is critical, as individuals with low
PA levels have a higher prevalence of sleep disorders, forming a ‘dual risk burden’ that may amplify
cardiovascular risk [13,14].
The limitations of current research on PA, sleep disorders, and hypertension are mainly that most
observational studies have small sample sizes, unmeasured confounding factors (e.g. socioeconomic
gradients, polygenic risk) and reverse causality (e.g. reduced PA in individuals with prehypertension)
undermine causal inference in traditional epidemiological designs, and existing genetic studies are
mainly ethnically focused on European populations with limited generalisability. These gaps highlight
the need for innovative approaches that combine large-scale observational data with causal inference
methods.
To address these challenges, we employed a dual analytical framework combining NHANES (2005–
2018) and two-sample MR. NHANES provides nationally representative data with detailed PA and
sleep assessments, enabling robust exploration of nonlinear associations and interaction effects. MR
analysis, using genetic variants as instrumental variables, allows causal inference approximating ran-
domised controlled trial conditions while minimising confounding [15].
Therefore, we first utilised data from NHANES to investigate the individual associations between
PA, sleep disorders, and hypertension, as well as their interaction on hypertension. Next, we examined
the causal relationships between PA, sleep disorders, and hypertension through MR analysis.
Methods
Overall study design
This study comprised two parts. First, we conducted an observational analysis using NHANES data
and weighted multivariate regression to examine the associations between PA, sleep disorders, and
hypertension, as well as their interaction, after adjusting for covariates. RCS analysis was also used
to explore the relationship between PA and hypertension. Second, we performed MR analysis using
BLOOD PRESSURE 3
summary statistics from genome-wide association studies (GWAS) to investigate the causal relation-
ships between different intensities of PA, sleep disorders, and hypertension.
Analysis based on NHANES data
NHANES sample population
We used NHANES data from 2005 to 2018, excluding the pandemic years of 2003–2004 and 2019–2020.
NHANES is an ongoing survey conducted by the US Centres for Disease Control and Prevention,
which uses a complex, multistage, stratified, and cluster probability design to select a representative
sample of the non-institutionalized US civilian population. The multistage design consists of four
stages: identifying counties, segments (city blocks), randomly selecting households within segments,
and randomly selecting individuals within households. NHANES data are provided every two years.
From 2005 to 2018, we combined seven successive NHANES cycles to create a large study sample.
For more information on the methodology and data collection used in NHANES, visit the following
website: (http://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes.htm).
This study included participants aged 18 years and older with information on PA and sleep disor-
ders. After excluding participants with missing covariate data(Supplementary Materials - NHANES
Data Definition), a total of 1,8052 subjects were included in the final analysis. The specific recruitment
process is shown in Figure 1. The Ethics Review Committee of the National Centre for Health
Statistics approved the survey protocol, and participants provided consent prior to data collection.
Data denitions and measurements
Blood pressure denition and measurement. Blood pressure measurements were taken three times
aer a ve-minute seated rest at the Mobile Examination Centre. Hypertension was classied based
on the average of the three measurements: systolic blood pressure of 130 mmHg or higher, or diastolic
blood pressure of 80 mmHg or higher [16]. Self-reported hypertension data from respondents were
also included [17,18].
Physical activity denition and measurement. PA data were collected using the WHO Global Physical
Activity Questionnaire [19]. Participants were asked about their physical activity in the past month [20].
Sleep disorder denition and measurement. Sleep disorders were assessed using the Sleep Disorder
Questionnaire, which asked whether participants had been diagnosed with a sleep disorder by a
doctor or medical professional [21].
Covariate information. Covariates included sex, age, BMI, race, education, income [22], alcohol
consumption, smoking history, diabetes, stroke, and depression.
Detailed definitions of these variables are provided in the supplementary materials.
NHANES data statistical analysis
Weighted multiple regression analysis. According to the NHANES analytical guidelines, the means
and standard errors (S.E.) of the measurement data are presented, with comparisons made between
hypertensive and non-hypertensive groups. Weighted t-tests were used to compare the hypertensive
and non-hypertensive groups. Categorical variables were evaluated using descriptive statistics based
on case numbers and weighted prevalence [n (weighted%)], with weights derived from NHANES
data. Chi-square tests were used to assess the variations between the hypertensive and non-hypertensive
groups. Multivariable logistic regression was used to examine the associations between PA, sleep
disorders, and their interactions with hypertension. Model 1, unadjusted for covariates, was used for
the analysis. Model 2 controlled for age, gender, and BMI. Model 3, in addition to the variables in
Model 2, also controlled for race, depression, education level, income, alcohol consumption, smoking
history, diabetes, and stroke. An additive model was developed to explore potential interactions,
4 B. QIU ETAL.
assessing whether the interaction eect of sleep disorders and PA on hypertension surpassed the sum
of their independent eects. R soware 4.2.0 was used for data analysis. A P value of less than 0.05
was considered statistically signicant.
RCS analysis.To explore potential nonlinear associations between PA and hypertension, RCS regression
analyses were performed using the rms package in R. e number and positions of knots were
automatically determined based on the distribution of PA levels. Analyses were conducted across
Models 1–3, with PA as the continuous independent variable and adjusted odds ratios (ORs) for
hypertension as the dependent variable, controlling for covariates specied in each model.
Mendelian randomization
Study design
We used a two-sample MR analysis to investigate the causal links between genetically predicted PA,
sleep disorders, and hypertension. (The analysis flowchart is shown in Figure 2). Our MR study
adhered to the STROBE-MR guidelines for strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in
Epidemiology using MR (Supplementary-Materials-STROBE).
Figure 1. Flowchart of participant selection in NHANES (2005–2018).
BLOOD PRESSURE 5
MR study population and data
Genetic variants associated with light, moderate, and vigorous PA, sleep disorders, and hypertension
were obtained from the MRC-IEU consortium. The hypertension dataset included 463,010 Europeans
(54,358 cases and 408,652 controls). Data for light PA (460,376 Europeans), moderate PA (440,266
Europeans), and vigorous PA (440,512 Europeans) were also included in the analysis. Insomnia data
were also included, with 462,341 Europeans. The genetic variation datasets for PA were sourced from
the GWAS Catalogue, including 89,683 Europeans and 8,669,219 SNPs (Supplementary Table 1). The
data were downloaded from the IEU Open GWAS database (https://gwas.mrcieu.ac.uk/). All studies
were reviewed and approved by local institutional review boards, and informed consent was obtained
from each participant.
Genetic variants with genome-wide significance (P = 5e-08) were selected for exposure, excluding
those in linkage disequilibrium (r
2
<0.001, 10,000 KB). Each SNP was checked using the PhenoScanner
database to exclude those significantly associated with potential confounders and other characteristics
related to PA and sleep disorders. Potential confounders, including age, gender, education, BMI,
depression, alcohol consumption, smoking, diabetes, and stroke, were considered in relation to
hypertension.
MR data statistical analysis
The primary method used to assess the causal relationships between the risk of hypertension, sleep
disorders, and genetically predicted levels of physical activity (light PA, moderate PA, and vigorous
PA) was the IVW approach. The IVW results were validated using MR methods such as MR-Egger,
weighted median, weighted mode, and MR-PRESSO. Sensitivity analyses were conducted to evaluate
potential directional pleiotropy affecting MR causal estimates by assessing the extent of bias intro-
duced by pleiotropic instruments. The Cochrane’s Q test was used to assess potential heterogeneity,
and random-effects IVW analyses adjusted for measured heterogeneity (p < 0.05). MR-Egger intercept
was used to estimate horizontal pleiotropy (p < 0.05 indicating potential presence). MR-PRESSO assessed
pleiotropy by comparing the observed and expected residual sum of squares.

Observational association between sleep disorders and hypertension
Participants with sleep disorders were more likely to develop hypertension than those without [adjusted
odds ratio (OR) 1.77, 95% CI 1.31–2.41 in Model 1; OR 1.76, 95% CI 1.23–2.53 in Model 2]. The
risk remained significant [Model 3 OR = 1.61, 95% CI 1.1–2.35] even after adjusting for factors such
as age, gender, BMI, race, education, income, alcohol use, smoking history, diabetes, stroke, and
depression. (Table 2).
Observational association between physical activity and hypertension
In Model 1, PA was negatively associated with hypertension [OR 0.85, 95% CI 0.79–0.90]. However,
this negative association disappeared after adjusting for other variables in Models 2 and 3. (Table 2).

Interaction between sleep disorder, physical activity, and hypertension
The interaction between sleep disorders and PA on hypertension was not significant in Models 1, 2,
and 3. (Table 2).
RCS analysis reveal the association between PA and hypertension
The results showed a significant non-linear dose-response association between PA and hypertension.
After adjusting for relevant covariates, the non-linear relationship remained significant in Models 2
and 3 (P-overall < 0.0001, P-non-linear < 0.0001). (The results are shown in Figure 3). As PA levels
increased, the risk of hypertension initially decreased significantly, suggesting that moderate PA plays
a crucial role in reducing hypertension risk. After reaching a minimum, the risk of hypertension
gradually increased, suggesting that excessive PA may negatively affect blood pressure control. As PA
levels continued to increase, the risk of hypertension slowly decreased, suggesting that at very high
levels of PA, the risk of hypertension gradually declines, but more slowly. This implies that the pro-
tective effect of excessive PA on hypertension may diminish.
Causal relationships between physical activity, sleep disorders, and hypertension
We used MR analysis of GWAS summary statistics to evaluate the causal effects of PA (light, mod-
erate, and vigorous) and sleep disorders on hypertension. IVW analysis revealed significant negative
causal relationships between light PA (OR = 0.870,95% CI 0.803–0.943, p = 0.0007) and vigorous PA
(OR = 0.964,95% CI 0.940–0.988, p = 0.004) and hypertension. In contrast, sleep disorders exhibited
a positive causal relationship (OR = 1.069,95% CI 1.032–1.107, p = 0.0002). No significant causal
relationship was found between moderate PA and hypertension. These findings were consistent across
various complementary MR methods(Supplementary Table 3), demonstrating robustness and reliabil-
ity(Table 3). Sensitivity analysis showed no evidence of pleiotropy or heterogeneity, and F statistics
of all instrumental variables are >10, indicating that the instrument strength is sufficient and can
effectively avoid weak instrument bias. (Supplementary Table 2). The instrumental variables used in
the MR analysis are listed in Supplementary Table 4.
Discussion
This study combines observational data from NHANES (2005–2018) with 18,052 individuals to explore
the associations and interactions between sleep difficulties, PA, and hypertension, supplemented by
a two-sample MR analysis.
Our analyses consistently identified a substantial positive correlation between hypertension and
sleep problems, which aligns with previous research [23,24]. For instance, Fiorentini et al. reported
a hypertension prevalence of 87.1% among individuals with poor sleep, compared to 35.1% among
those with good sleep [25] and a meta-analysis further confirmed this relationship [26].
The relationship between PA and hypertension proved more complex. While an unadjusted model
suggested a significant negative correlation, this association was attenuated after adjustment for

covariates, underscoring the confounding nature of this relationship. To elucidate the underlying
dose-response pattern, we employed RCS analysis, which revealed a significant non-linear, S-shaped
relationship (P-non-linear < 0.001). This suggests that moderate PA is effective in preventing and
controlling hypertension [7,27], but excessively high levels may attenuate these benefits or negatively
affect blood pressure control, underscoring the importance of personalised exercise prescriptions. It
is important to note that RCS analysis reflects population-level trends, and individual variability must
be considered. Previous studies have highlighted that this dose-response relationship may be influ-
enced by factors such as sex, age, race, and BMI [28. Sleep disorders and PA are linked, and their
interaction effect on hypertension warrants further investigation. Therefore, in our observational study,
we performed multiple regression analysis and found no significant correlation. This result may be
due to the fact that sleep disorders and PA each have distinct effects on hypertension, but when
combined, they may offset or weaken each other’s effects. Specifically, PA may lower blood pressure
via endothelial nitric oxide synthase activation and improved arterial compliance [29] whereas sleep
disorders elevate blood pressure through sympathetic overactivation and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal
axis dysregulation [30]. These independent mechanisms likely result in additive rather than synergistic
effects. Future studies should investigate shared mediators (e.g. inflammatory markers) to clarify
potential mechanistic overlaps. We acknowledge that while the use of self-reported, semi-quantitative
PA categories (light, moderate, and vigorous intensity) may introduce heterogeneity within each
intensity group—particularly for vigorous-intensity PA where individual interpretations can vary sub-
stantially—the large sample size of the NHANES cohort effectively mitigates the impact of such
measurement variability, thereby enhancing the reliability of the observed associations.
The two-sample MR analysis provided complementary genetic evidence, revealing significant causal
effects of light and vigorous PA on hypertension reduction, but no significant direct causal effect for
moderate PA. This discrepancy with the observational findings—which showed a nonlinear dose-response
relationship—highlights both the methodological complementarity and distinct mechanistic pathways
underlying different PA intensities. The null association for moderate PA in MR analyses may be
explained by several interrelated factors. Biologically, while light and vigorous PA may influence
hypertension through more direct hemodynamic mechanisms (e.g. shear-mediated endothelial adap-
tation) [31], moderate PA likely exerts its benefits largely through indirect pathways such as weight
loss, improved insulin sensitivity, and reduced systemic inflammation [32]. Since MR estimates the
direct causal effect of an exposure, effects mediated substantially through intermediate metabolic
pathways may not be fully captured. Methodologically, genetic instruments for PA primarily reflect
lifelong activity propensities [33], in contrast to self-reported questionnaire data that capture
shorter-term behavioural patterns. This measurement difference, combined with the limited general-
isability of GWAS data derived predominantly from European-ancestry populations [34], may further
contribute to the attenuated genetic signal specifically for moderate-intensity activity. Thus, the
apparent discordance between MR and observational results underscores the complementary insights
offered by each method: MR prioritises lifelong, genetically proxied causal effects with reduced con-
founding, whereas observational analyses capture near-term behavioural patterns and net effects—
including those mediated through intermediate metabolic pathways [31]. Integrating both frameworks
is critical to reconcile genetic and environmental contributions to hypertension [35]. A key strength
of this study is the integration of NHANES observational data (2005–2018) with MR methods. This
comprehensive approach allowed for the evaluation of various influencing factors and a large sample
size, enabling effective adjustment and analysis of multiple confounders in multivariable regression
models. This provided sufficient statistical power to assess the causal relationships between PA, sleep

disorders, and hypertension. Additionally, MR methods help avoid biases from unmeasured confounders
and reverse causality.
Our study has several limitations. When analysing the NHANES database, data constraints, the
influence of medication interventions, and uncontrolled confounding factors contributed to variability
in blood pressure outcomes [36]. The absence of a significant association between PA and hyperten-
sion after covariate adjustment further underscores the complexity of this relationship. Second, while
our MR analysis found no significant causal relationship between moderate-intensity PA and hyper-
tension—contrary to some clinical studies—this discrepancy highlights the need for more rigorously
controlled studies to clarify these associations. Third, our definition of sleep disorders relied on
physician diagnoses rather than quantitative measures of sleep duration or quality. This approach
likely underestimates the true prevalence of sleep disturbances and precluded exploration of the
established U-shaped relationship between sleep duration and hypertension risk, potentially constrain-
ing our ability to fully elucidate the interplay between sleep, PA, and hypertension. Future studies
using objective sleep measurements are warranted to address this gap.
Conclusion
Our study provides three key advances to hypertension prevention. First, an S-shaped dose-response
relationship between PA and hypertension, challenging current linear guidelines. Second, Mendelian
randomisation analyses confirmed causal roles of light and vigorous PA, while highlighting the need
to re-evaluate moderate-intensity recommendations. Third, the identification of sleep disorders as an
independent risk factor, with PA and sleep acting through distinct biological pathways rather than
synergistically. These findings support integrated yet distinct intervention strategies. Future efforts
should prioritise personalised PA prescriptions and trials to establish optimal activity thresholds and
combined lifestyle interventions.
